flaw.ctx: You asked for an async read-through cache.
flaw.answer: `Release()` is not in a `finally`. When the load throws, the semaphore is **never released** — every later call waits forever. One failed load and the cache is dead. It also serialises every load behind one semaphore, so one slow key blocks all keys.
flaw.fix: `try { … } finally { _gate.Release(); }`; better, cache `Lazy<Task<T>>` per key (no global gate) and evict faulted tasks so a failure is retried.

qa.a: O(1) average for lookup, insert, remove; O(n) worst case if many keys collide. Enumeration is O(n) and order is not guaranteed.

Separate chaining, but without node objects: an `int[] buckets` of indices into an `Entry[]` array, each entry carrying its hash, key, value and a `next` index. Colliding keys form a chain through `next`.

When the entries array is full it grows to a larger prime (about double) and every entry is rehashed into new buckets — O(n) for that insert, amortised O(1). Pre-size with the constructor capacity when you know n.
Removing does not shrink anything: freed slots go on a free list for reuse. `TrimExcess()` shrinks. A struct key that is large is copied into every entry.

Only code that locks the *same object*. `lock (x)` is `Monitor.Enter/Exit` on x's object header, in a try/finally. It also acts as a full memory barrier, so writes inside are visible to the next locker.
Yes, with two locks taken in different orders (D5), or with a call out to unknown code while holding the lock. One lock and no callouts cannot deadlock. `Monitor` is re-entrant for the same thread.

Uncontended, a lock is tens of nanoseconds. Contended, threads spin briefly then block, causing context switches; throughput collapses toward one thread's worth. The fix is less work under the lock, or more locks (striping).
`this`, a `Type`, a string — other code can lock them too. Use a private readonly object (or `System.Threading.Lock` in .NET 9+).

qa.q: Does async create a new thread?
qa.a: No. `async` lets a method be suspended; `await` on an incomplete task returns to the caller and schedules the rest as a continuation. No thread exists for the waiting.

The OS completes the I/O (I/O completion ports on Windows, epoll on Linux) and the continuation is queued to the thread pool or the captured context. The thread was free the whole time — that is the point.

Cooperatively. You pass a `CancellationToken` down; APIs that accept it observe it and throw `OperationCanceledException`. Nothing is aborted from outside. Blocked primitives need a registration to wake them (BoundedBlockingQueue does this).

qa.q: Can you await inside a lock?
qa.a: No — the compiler forbids it, because the continuation may run on another thread. Use `SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync` with `Release` in a `finally` (R12 is what happens without the finally).

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Given:
> 
> interface Task {
>     String getId();
>     List<Task> getSubTasks();
> }
> 
> A task depends on completion of all subtasks.
> 
> Implement:
> 
> addTask(Task t)
> 
> Throws if adding the task creates a cycle.
> 
> pollNextTask()
> 
> Returns the next executable task whose dependencies are completed.

A work queue that understands dependencies. Tasks arrive with their subtasks, a task cannot run until all its subtasks have, and a dependency that would make progress impossible must be rejected at the moment it is introduced.

Not a value — a component with three or four operations. The interesting parts are cycle detection on insert, and the atomicity of a rejected insert.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
**The interface cannot work as given, and saying so is the question.**

`pollNextTask()` returns a task whose dependencies are complete. Nothing in the interface ever says a task *became* complete. So the first call returns a leaf, and every subsequent call returns either the same leaf forever or nothing — the system cannot make progress. A `CompleteTask(id)` (or a callback, or having `pollNextTask` mark the task complete on return) is required, and which one you pick changes the semantics.

I add `CompleteTask(string id)` and say why. Two smaller gaps follow from it: does `pollNextTask` hand the same task out twice if it is called twice before completion (I say no, tracked by an issued set), and what happens if a worker takes a task and dies (I add `RequeueTask`, because without it the task is lost forever).

Also: **what does `addTask` do if the task is already registered with different subtasks?** I union the edges, and refuse if the task has already been issued — see the follow-up, because this is where the real bug was.

| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| `CompleteTask(id)` exists, because the interface as given cannot make progress. | Without it, `pollNextTask` returns the first leaf and nothing ever unblocks. **This is the clarification to raise before writing any code.** |
| `pollNextTask` issues each task at most once. | Otherwise two workers polling concurrently both run the same task. Tracked with an issued set; a dropped task needs an explicit `RequeueTask`. |
| Ids are unique and identify a task; the object is incidental. | Two `Task` objects with the same id are the same task. That is what lets a cycle be closed across two `addTask` calls with different objects. |
| Re-adding a registered task unions its dependencies. | The alternative — first registration wins — silently ignores what the caller asked for. Unioning is the defensible choice, and it is what exposed a real bug; see the follow-up. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
Three observations, and only the first is the algorithm.

**One: it is a dependency graph, so readiness is an in-degree count.** A task is runnable when the number of its subtasks that are not yet complete reaches zero. Keep that count per task, keep a reverse map from each subtask to the tasks waiting on it, and completing a task is a decrement of each waiter — O(1) per edge, and any waiter that hits zero goes on the ready queue. That is Kahn’s algorithm, run incrementally instead of in a batch.

**Two: cycle detection is on insert, which is a different problem from topological sorting.** A batch topological sort detects a cycle by *failing to sort* — if fewer than n tasks come out, there was a cycle. That does not work here, because the graph is built incrementally and you must reject at the moment the bad edge is added. So it needs an explicit directed cycle check: three-colour DFS, where grey means "on the current path" and meeting grey is a back edge.

**Three, and this is the staff-level part: the insert must be atomic.** Check the whole merged graph first, commit second. It is tempting to register as you walk and unwind on failure, and unwinding is exactly where the bug lives — a partially-registered rejected task leaves the manager in a state no caller can reason about. Collect into locals, validate, and only then touch the fields. Then nothing after the validation can fail, so there is nothing to unwind.

And the reason the cycle check must run over the **union** of the existing and new edges rather than the new ones alone: a cycle can be closed by an edge whose other half was added in an earlier call. That is not hypothetical — my first implementation overwrote the existing edges instead of unioning them, and that exact case passed silently.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** Store the tasks. On `pollNextTask`, run a full topological sort over the whole graph and return the first task whose dependencies are all complete. Detect cycles then, by the sort failing. *`addTask` O(1), `pollNextTask` O(V + E). Space O(V + E).*

**Why not good enough.** Two problems, and the second is the real one. The performance objection is that `pollNextTask` is the hot operation — called once per task — so an O(V+E) poll makes the whole run O(V·(V+E)). The **correctness** objection is that the specification says `addTask` throws on a cycle, and deferring detection to poll time means the bad edge has already been accepted: the caller gets no error at the point where they could still do something about it, and by the time poll fails you cannot tell which of the accepted tasks caused it.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | `AddTask(ITask)`, `PollNextTask()`, `CompleteTask(id)` |
| TRANSFORMATION | The task closure is walked into id-keyed nodes and edges; readiness becomes an outstanding-dependency count |
| DATA STRUCTURE | Five dictionaries and a queue: tasks, dependsOn, blocks (reverse), outstanding, plus `_ready`, `_queued`, `_issued`, `_completed` |
| ALGORITHM | Collect → cycle-check the merged graph → commit. Completion decrements waiters and enqueues those reaching zero. |
| OUTPUT | A runnable task, or null; `CycleException` on a cycle |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- **Phase 1** — walk the new task’s closure into local `newTasks` and `newEdges`. Touch no fields.
- **Phase 2** — build `merged` as the **union** of existing and new edges; run the three-colour DFS from the new task’s id; throw `CycleException` if a back edge is found.
- Also refuse if a new edge would be added to a task already issued or completed — ambiguous, so reject rather than guess.
- **Phase 3** — commit. Register unseen tasks, then add each new edge, updating `_blocks` and `_outstanding`.
- Mark ready any task whose outstanding count is zero.
- `PollNextTask`: pop from `_ready`, skipping completed, still-blocked, or already-issued entries.
- `CompleteTask`: idempotent; decrement each waiter and mark ready at zero.

- Cycle detection happens on **`addTask`**, not at execution time. That is the design difference from a batch topological sort and it is what the question is about.
- A rejected `addTask` must leave the manager exactly as it was. Half-applying a change and then throwing is worse than not validating.
- Subtasks arrive as objects, so the whole reachable closure gets registered, not just the top task.
- A task reachable by two paths is one task, registered once.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| `_dependsOn` and `_blocks`, both directions | `_dependsOn` is needed for the cycle check; `_blocks` is needed so completion is O(waiters) rather than a scan of every task. Keeping both is the standard cost of incremental readiness. |
| `_outstanding` count per task | The in-degree, restricted to incomplete dependencies. A set of incomplete dependencies would also work and costs more memory for no extra capability. |
| `Queue` plus a `_queued` set | The queue gives FIFO fairness among ready tasks. The set stops a task being queued twice, which becomes possible once edges can be added to an already-ready task. |
| `_issued` separate from `_completed` | A task handed to a worker is neither ready nor done. Without the distinction, two polls return the same task and two workers run it. |
| Three-colour DFS for the cycle check | Grey = on the current path, black = finished and clean. Re-entering a **black** node must not be a failure — that is a diamond, not a cycle — and conflating the two is the classic error here. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**The three phases, and why the order is the design.** Phase 1 collects into locals. Phase 2 validates. Phase 3 commits, and **nothing in phase 3 can fail** — it is only dictionary writes. So a rejected `addTask` cannot leave the manager half-updated, and there is no unwind path to get wrong. The test asserts `TaskCount` is unchanged after every throw, because this property is invisible otherwise.

**The union in phase 2 — where the real bug was.** `foreach (string d in kv.Value) if (!deps.Contains(d)) deps.Add(d);` rather than `merged[kv.Key] = kv.Value`. Assignment dropped an existing task’s original edges, so a cycle closed across two calls went undetected. **This was found by a test, not by reading.** The comment in the code says so, because a future reader will otherwise be tempted to simplify it back.

**Refusing a new dependency on an issued task.** If a task has already been handed to a worker and someone adds a dependency to it, should it re-run? There is no good answer, so it throws `InvalidOperationException`. The check sits in phase 2, before any commit, so the refusal is atomic like the cycle rejection. Guessing either way here would be worse than refusing.

**`MarkReady` and the `_queued` set.** A task can reach zero outstanding dependencies more than once — add an edge, complete it, add another. Without `_queued`, it would sit in `_ready` twice and `PollNextTask` would hand it out twice. The `_issued` check inside `MarkReady` covers the other direction.

**Why `PollNextTask` re-verifies.** It skips entries that are completed, still blocked, or already issued. Entries in `_ready` can go stale: a task queued as ready can gain a dependency before it is polled. Re-checking `_outstanding[id] > 0` at the point of use is cheaper and more robust than trying to remove it from the middle of the queue.

**`CompleteTask` is idempotent.** `if (!_completed.Add(id)) return;` — a retried completion, which any distributed worker will eventually send, must not decrement the waiters twice. Double-decrementing would drive `_outstanding` negative and a task would become ready before its dependencies finished: silent, and catastrophic.

**`Collect` is iterative on purpose.** An explicit `Stack<ITask>` rather than recursion, because dependency chains are exactly the shape that gets deep. Note that `FindCycleFrom` **is** recursive, which is the standard shape for three-colour DFS and is the one place a very deep graph could still overflow — worth naming rather than claiming the whole class is stack-safe.

**`FindCycleFrom` returns the cycle, not a bool.** `path.IndexOf(path[^1])` trims the trailing tail so the exception names the actual loop. "There is a cycle" is not actionable; "a → b → c → a" is. It costs a list and it is what makes the error message worth reading.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `AddTask` | O(Vₙ + Eₘ) | O(V + E) | Collects the new closure, then DFS over the merged graph |
| `PollNextTask` | O(1) amortised | O(1) | Pops until a valid entry; each is skipped once |
| `CompleteTask` | O(waiters) | O(1) | One decrement per task blocked on it |
| whole run | O(V + E) total for polls and completions | O(V + E) | Each edge relaxed exactly once across the run |
| `RequeueTask` | O(1) | O(1) | Clears the issued flag and re-queues |

**The cycle check dominates `AddTask` and it is not free.** It is O(V + E) over the merged graph each time, so adding n tasks one at a time is O(n(V+E)) overall — worse than the single O(V+E) of a batch topological sort. That is the price of rejecting at insert time, and it is the right price because the alternative is accepting a cycle you cannot attribute. Restricting the DFS to the component reachable from the new task, which is what the code does, keeps it proportional to the affected subgraph rather than the whole manager — worth saying, because it is the difference between acceptable and not.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Null task | Throws `ArgumentNullException`. |
| Null id | Throws during `Collect`, before any commit. |
| Self-dependency | `CycleException`. Caught by the grey check with no special case. |
| Cycle within one `addTask` | Caught; nothing registered. |
| **Cycle across two `addTask` calls** | Caught, because the check runs over the union. The bug case. |
| Diamond (two paths to one task) | Registered once, and completing it unblocks both parents. Must **not** be reported as a cycle — that is the grey-versus-black distinction. |
| `pollNextTask` with nothing runnable | Returns null. Note that null does not distinguish "blocked" from "finished"; a caller needing that should check `TaskCount` against completed. |
| Polling the same task twice | Issued once. `RequeueTask` is the way back. |
| `CompleteTask` on an unknown id | Throws `KeyNotFoundException`. |
| `CompleteTask` twice | Idempotent — the second is a no-op, and must be. |
| Adding a dependency to an issued task | Refused, rather than guessed at. |
| A very deep chain | `Collect` is iterative and safe; the recursive cycle check is the remaining depth risk. |

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**Several workers poll concurrently. Make it safe.**

One lock around each public method is the right first answer: the critical sections are dictionary operations, so they are short. The `_issued` set is what makes concurrent polling correct — without it two workers get the same task.

For throughput, `_ready` could be a `BlockingCollection` so workers block instead of polling and getting null, which also removes a busy-wait loop from every caller.

*Trade-off:* A single lock serialises polls, which is unlikely to matter because the tasks themselves are the expensive part. Finer-grained locking is genuinely hard here: the invariant spans four dictionaries, so per-task locks would need a consistent acquisition order to avoid deadlock, and the ready-queue transition would still need to be atomic with the outstanding-count decrement. I would take the single lock and measure.

**A worker takes a task and dies. What happens?**

`RequeueTask(id)` clears the issued flag and re-queues if the dependencies are still satisfied. To detect the death rather than be told about it, issue a lease with a deadline and requeue automatically when it expires — which needs a timer, and that timer is Q7.

*Trade-off:* Explicit requeue is simple and needs a cooperative worker or a supervisor. Leases are automatic and introduce **at-least-once** execution: a slow worker can have its lease expire while still running, so the task runs twice. That forces tasks to be idempotent, which is a requirement on the caller rather than on this class, and it should be stated as such rather than hidden.

**A task fails. Should its dependents run?**

`FailTask(id)` with a policy. **Abort**: mark the whole dependent subtree unrunnable and report it, which is what a build system does — a failed compile must not produce a deploy. **Retry**: requeue with a backoff and an attempt limit, then abort. **Continue**: treat failure as completion, which is almost always wrong and occasionally right for optional work.

*Trade-off:* Abort is the safe default and it needs a reverse traversal to find everything downstream, which `_blocks` already supports. Retry needs the attempt count and a timer. I would implement abort, expose the policy as a parameter, and say clearly that treating a failure as a completion is the one option I would not offer without the caller asking for it by name.

**Why detect the cycle on insert rather than at execution time?**

Insert-time detection gives an error **at the point where the caller can act on it** — they are holding the task that caused it, and the exception can name the loop. Execution-time detection means the bad edge was accepted, so the failure surfaces later, in a different stack, attributed to nothing in particular; and by then you cannot tell which of the accepted tasks was at fault.

*Trade-off:* The cost is O(V + E) per add instead of once, making n adds O(n(V+E)) rather than O(V+E). Restricting the DFS to the reachable component keeps that proportional to the affected subgraph. If adds were extremely hot and cycles genuinely impossible by construction, batching the validation would be defensible — but the specification says `addTask` throws, so it is not an option here.

**Priorities: some ready tasks matter more than others.**

Replace `_ready` with a priority queue keyed on priority. Readiness logic is untouched — only the order among already-ready tasks changes.

*Trade-off:* O(log n) instead of O(1) per poll, which is irrelevant next to running the task. The real consequence is **starvation**: a steady stream of high-priority tasks can keep a low-priority one waiting forever. Ageing — raising effective priority with waiting time — is the standard fix, and mentioning starvation unprompted is the signal here, because the data-structure swap is trivial and the fairness problem is not.
